From 6d99479799c69c3cb588fcda19c81d8f61d64ecd Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Qing Wang <wangqing7171@gmail.com>
Date: Tue, 2 Jun 2026 11:08:54 +0800
Subject: [PATCH] rseq: Fix using an uninitialized stack variable in
 rseq_exit_user_update()

There is an bug in which an uninitialized stack variable is used in
rseq_exit_user_update() as reported by syzbot:

BUG: KMSAN: kernel-infoleak in rseq_set_ids_get_csaddr include/linux/rseq_entry.h:502 [inline]

The local variable:

	struct rseq_ids ids = {
		.cpu_id	 = task_cpu(t),
		.mm_cid	 = task_mm_cid(t),
		.node_id = cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id),
	};

According to the C standard, the evaluation order of expressions in an
initializer list is indeterminately sequenced. The compiler (Clang, in
this KMSAN build) evaluates `cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id)` *before*
`ids.cpu_id` is initialized with `task_cpu(t)`.

This is fixed by moving the assignment of ids.node_id outside the
structure initialization.

Fixes: 82f572449cfe ("rseq: Implement read only ABI enforcement for optimized RSEQ V2 mode")
Closes: https://syzkaller.appspot.com/bug?extid=185a631927096f9da2fc
Reported-by: syzbot+185a631927096f9da2fc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Qing Wang <wangqing7171@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Acked-by: Mark Rutland <mark.rutland@arm.com>
Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260602030854.574038-1-wangqing7171@gmail.com

diff --git a/include/linux/rseq_entry.h b/include/linux/rseq_entry.h
index 63bc72086e75..ed9da6e41a2a 100644
--- a/include/linux/rseq_entry.h
+++ b/include/linux/rseq_entry.h
@@ -635,10 +635,11 @@ static __always_inline bool rseq_exit_user_update(struct pt_regs *regs, struct t
 		return true;
 	}
 
+	int cpu = task_cpu(t);
 	struct rseq_ids ids = {
-		.cpu_id	 = task_cpu(t),
+		.cpu_id	 = cpu,
 		.mm_cid	 = task_mm_cid(t),
-		.node_id = cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id),
+		.node_id = cpu_to_node(cpu),
 	};
 
 	return rseq_update_usr(t, regs, &ids);
-- 
2.34.1

The patch modifies a single file, `include/linux/rseq_entry.h`, to fix a bug where an uninitialized stack variable was used in `rseq_exit_user_update()`. The bug occurred because the initializer list of the `struct rseq_ids ids` variable used `ids.cpu_id` (which itself is being initialized) to compute `ids.node_id`, leading to indeterminately sequenced evaluation and use of an uninitialized value. The fix introduces a separate local variable `cpu` to hold the value of `task_cpu(t)` before the struct initialization, then uses this variable for both `cpu_id` and `node_id` fields.

**Modifications in `include/linux/rseq_entry.h`**:
- Added a local variable declaration: `int cpu = task_cpu(t);` before the `struct rseq_ids ids` declaration.
- Changed the initializer for `ids.cpu_id` from `task_cpu(t)` to `cpu`.
- Changed the initializer for `ids.node_id` from `cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id)` to `cpu_to_node(cpu)`.

**Relationships between modifications**:
- The new variable `cpu` acts as a single source of truth for both `cpu_id` and `node_id` calculations. By evaluating `task_cpu(t)` only once and storing it in `cpu`, the fix ensures that the `node_id` computation uses a properly initialized value, avoiding dependency on the initialization order within the struct initializer list. This eliminates the undefined behavior and the kernel infoleak reported by syzbot.

Root cause:
The initializer list for struct rseq_ids in rseq_exit_user_update() uses ids.cpu_id to compute ids.node_id, but the C standard does not guarantee evaluation order, so ids.cpu_id may not be initialized when cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id) is evaluated, leading to use of an uninitialized stack variable.

Code statements information:
The code statements that lead to the bug are:
```
struct rseq_ids ids = {
    .cpu_id  = task_cpu(t),
    .mm_cid  = task_mm_cid(t),
    .node_id = cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id),
};
```
Reason:
In this initializer list, the expression `cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id)` depends on `ids.cpu_id`, but the C standard does not guarantee the evaluation order of initializer elements. The compiler may evaluate `cpu_to_node(ids.cpu_id)` before `ids.cpu_id` is assigned `task_cpu(t)`, causing `ids.cpu_id` to be uninitialized (or containing a stale value) at that point. This leads to using an uninitialized stack variable, as detected by KMSAN.

The code statements that fix the bug are:
```
int cpu = task_cpu(t);
struct rseq_ids ids = {
    .cpu_id  = cpu,
    .mm_cid  = task_mm_cid(t),
    .node_id = cpu_to_node(cpu),
};
```
Reason:
The fix decouples the initialization order dependency by computing `task_cpu(t)` into a local variable `cpu` before the struct initialization. Then both `ids.cpu_id` and `ids.node_id` use this already-initialized `cpu` value, eliminating any reliance on the indeterminate evaluation order of initializer elements. This ensures that `cpu_to_node()` always receives a valid, initialized argument.
